chunks.raw_text: Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) is the sudden loss of all heart activity due to an irregular heart rhythm, accounting for about 20% of fatalities in developed countries. Detecting SCA early is challenging because it occurs suddenly and unpredictably. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) provide valuable heart activity data utilized by Machine Learning (ML) models to predict known conditions like arrhythmias, rather than predicting cardiac arrest risk. Additionally, these ML models typically rely on the full 12-lead ECGs, which are impractical for wearable devices. The proposed method in this study utilizes a pretrained deep-learning model to predict cardiac arrest risk using reduced-lead ECG data. The final model, adapted to work with 6-lead input derived from the MUSIC and I-Care datasets, achieved an AUCROC (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristics) of 0.8851 and an F1-score of 0.8334, demonstrating that reduced-lead ECG could effectively classify cardiac arrest risk.

chunks.raw_text: **Keywords:** Sudden Cardiac Death, Sudden Cardiac Arrest Risk Classification, Trans

Sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) is a leading cause of mortality worldwide, with approximately 350,000 out-of-hospital cases annually in the U.S. [1]. In Canada, SCA incidence ranges between 53 and 59 per 100,000 individuals annually, with low survival rates (4.3%–9.0%) after hospital discharge [2]. Due to its unpredictability, early risk classification is critical for improving survival outcomes [3]. Electrocardiograms (ECGs) are widely used for cardiac health assessment and detecting arrhythmias. However, manual ECG interpretation is time-consuming and prone to errors, even among experienced clinicians. A systematic review highlighted frequent disagreements in physician ECG interpretations, underscoring the need for automated diagnostic solutions [4]. Recent advancements in deep learning (DL) have demonstrated high-accuracy ECG classification, often outperforming human cardiologists [5]. However, most deep learning models were designed to diagnose known conditions such as arrhythmias and myocardial infarction rather than predict SCA risk [6]. Existing DL models for ECG analysis typically rely on full 12-lead ECG recordings, which are impractical for wearable devices and emergency settings. While wearable ECG devices (e.g., single-lead and 3-lead configurations) offer greater accessibility, they often have reduced diagnostic capabilities compared to standard 12-lead systems [7]. Additionally, training deep learning models for risk classification requires large annotated datasets, which are expensive and difficult to obtain, particularly for rare cardiac events [8]. A scalable and data-efficient approach is essential for deploying multi-lead ECG-based cardiac arrest prediction models in clinical and wearable settings.

chunks.raw_text: Deep learning models have gained popularity in different areas, including healthcare [9– 11] and industrial [12, 13] applications. Transfer learning (TL), a technique where models trained on large datasets are adapted for new tasks, offers a promising solution. While widely applied in image and speech recognition, its use in ECG-based risk classification remains underexplored [14]. Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of TL for ECG analysis. For instance, TL significantly improved single-lead ECG arrhythmia detection over training from scratch [15]. However, applying TL for SCA risk classification with multi-lead ECG remains an open problem. This study addresses these gaps by investigating whether transfer learning can enhance SCA risk classification using multi-lead ECG data, specifically single-lead and three-lead ECG configurations. A pre-trained ResNet-based deep learning model, originally developed for 12-lead ECG classification, is fine-tuned to classify cardiac arrest risk using reducedlead ECG data. To enhance generalization, we integrate two PhysioNet datasets, MUSIC (MUerte Subita en Insuficiencia Cardiaca) [16] and I-Care (International Cardiac Arrest REsearch consortium database) [17]. These datasets are combined to address issues such as class imbalance, variations in lead configurations, and signal fragmentation, creating a more diverse and robust training set. In addition to applying TL, a model is trained from scratch on the same dataset to establish a baseline for comparison. The results demonstrate that TL significantly outperforms training from scratch, achieving a higher AUC (0.8851 vs. 0.8112) and F1-score (0.8334 vs. 0.7921). These findings confirm that leveraging pre-trained features enhances performance and generalization when working with limited ECG data, making TL a promising approach for risk classification in wearable and clinical settings. The findings of this study highlight the potential for TL to improve multi-lead ECG-based risk classification, with applications in both wearable cardiac monitoring devices and clinical environments.

chunks.raw_text: Deep learning has revolutionized ECG analysis by enabling automated detection of cardiac abnormalities with high accuracy. Acharya et al. (2017) proposed a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for arrhythmia detection using single-lead ECGs, achieving an accuracy of 94% [18]. To address temporal dependencies in ECG signals, Yildirim et al. (2019) employed Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks for arrhythmia classification [19]. While effective, LSTMs are computationally intensive, requiring significant hardware resources and training time. Recent advancements have focused on improving computational efficiency and generalizability. For instance, Li et al. (2022) proposed a lightweight CNN architecture optimized for real-time arrhythmia detection on wearable devices, achieving comparable performance to traditional models with significantly lower computational costs [20]. Similarly, Zhang et al. (2023) introduced a hybrid model combining CNNs and attention mechanisms to improve arrhythmia detection in noisy ECG signals, demonstrating robustness in real-world scenarios [21]. These studies address the computational challenges of deep learning models, making them more suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments.

chunks.raw_text: Transfer learning has emerged as a powerful approach to address data and computational limitations in ECG analysis. By leveraging pre-trained models, TL reduces the need for large datasets and extensive computational resources. Hannun et al. (2019) developed a deep neural network for arrhythmia classification using single-lead ECG, achieving performance comparable to cardiologists [22]. Their work demonstrated the feasibility of applying deep learning to ambulatory ECG data, which is often limited in quantity. Similarly, Che et al. (2020) applied TL to detect arrhythmia and myocardial infarction, showing improved performance on smaller datasets [23]. Also, Wang et al. (2022) demonstrated the effectiveness of transfer learning for detecting myocardial infarction using 3-lead ECGs, achieving an AUC of 0.92 [24]. Their work underscores the potential of TL in scenarios where data is limited or only reduced-lead ECGs are available. Additionally, Chen et al. (2023) proposed a novel TL framework that adapts pre-trained models from 12-lead to single-lead ECG data, achieving state-of-the-art performance in arrhythmia detection [15]. These advancements highlight the potential of TL in addressing the challenges of ECG analysis.

chunks.raw_text: Cardiac arrest risk classification remains an underexplored area in ECG analysis, despite its potential to save lives through early detection and intervention. Attia et al. (2019) demonstrated the utility of deep learning for risk stratification by predicting atrial fibrillation from ECG [25]. While their study focused on atrial fibrillation, it showcased the broader potential of deep learning for identifying high-risk patients. Raju et al. (2021) proposed a CNN for sudden cardiac death prediction using 12-lead ECGs, achieving an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.87 [26]. This study highlighted the importance of leveraging multilead ECG data for risk prediction. In contrast, Ebrahimzadeh et al. (2020) used Heart Rate Variability (HRV) features for risk stratification, but their reliance on HRV limited the generalizability of their approach [27]. Recent research has begun to address the gap in cardiac arrest risk classification using reduced-lead ECGs. For instance, Kumar et al. (2022) developed a TL-based model for predicting sudden cardiac death using single-lead ECG, achieving an AUC of 0.85 [28]. Their work demonstrates the feasibility of applying advanced machine-learning techniques to reduced-lead data. These studies highlight the potential of integrating diverse data sources to improve risk stratification models.

Addressing these challenges through transfer learning approaches tailored for cardiac arrest classification could improve early detection and intervention strategies, potentially saving lives.

chunks.raw_text: This study uses two publicly available datasets on PhysioNet: MUSIC and I-Care. These datasets are chosen for their relevance to cardiac arrest prediction and their complementary characteristics, enabling a robust evaluation of the proposed model.

chunks.raw_text: The MUSIC dataset comprises high-resolution, three-lead ECG recordings from patients with chronic heart failure as part of a multi-center study on sudden cardiac death (SCD). Each patient is assigned a binary label: No-risk, indicating survival throughout the study period, or At-risk, indicating that the patient experienced SCD. These labels were derived from the subject metadata using the “Cause of death” field. All ECG signals were recorded at a sampling rate of 1000 Hz, providing high temporal resolution for detecting subtle abnormalities. In total, the dataset contains 554 ECG recordings. It was split into a training set of 443 samples and a test set of 111 samples. The training set includes 387 No-risk recordings (87.36%), and 56 At-risk recordings (12.64%), while the test set comprises 97 Norisk (87.39%), and 14 At-risk (12.61%) recordings. This imbalance posed a challenge during model training, as it could lead to bias toward the majority class. Initial efforts to correct this via random oversampling of the minority class led to overfitting. To mitigate this, the dataset was augmented with additional At-risk samples from the I-Care dataset, enhancing minority class representation and enhancing the model’s ability to learn discriminative features.

chunks.raw_text: The I-Care dataset consists of 413 single-lead ECG recordings obtained from intensive care unit (ICU) patients identified as being at risk of cardiac arrest. Unlike the MUSIC dataset, the I-Care dataset includes only At-risk patients, making it a valuable resource for augmenting the minority class in the MUSIC dataset. These recordings were split into a training set of 330 samples and a test set of 83 samples. The ECG signals in I-Care were recorded at a sampling rate of 500 Hz. Following integration with the MUSIC dataset, the final training set included 773 samples—387 No-risk and 386 At-risk—while the final test set consisted of 194 samples, evenly split between 97 No-risk and 97 At-risk. This integration mitigated the class imbalance and contributed to the development of a more generalizable and robust classification model.

chunks.raw_text: The raw ECG data underwent several key steps to improve consistency and performance. A 4th-order Butterworth bandpass filter with a frequency range of 0.5–50 Hz is applied to remove baseline wander and high-frequency noise while preserving clinically relevant features, using zero-phase filtering to avoid signal distortion. The signals are resampled to a target rate of 400 Hz, ensuring uniformity across datasets with different original sampling rates (500 Hz for I-Care and 1000 Hz for MUSIC). To handle varying signal lengths, the ECG data is truncated or zero-padded to a fixed length of 4096 samples, corresponding to approximately 10 seconds of data at 400 Hz, capturing multiple cardiac cycles. The zscore normalization is applied to standardize the amplitude distribution, improving training stability. The I-Care dataset contains multiple ECG files per patient, and the signals are concatenated before pre-processing to create a continuous representation that addresses the fragmented nature of the recordings. The preprocessed data is saved along with metadata, including patient ID, processed sampling rate, signal length, and cardiac arrest risk labels. This preprocessing pipeline is informed by the base model’s requirements, ensuring compatibility with its input specifications. It addresses common challenges in ECG data, such as noise removal, varying sampling rates, and fragmented recordings. Figure 1 illustrates a 10-second segment of raw ECG signals with visible baseline wander and noise to highlight the necessity of preprocessing. These distortions make direct model training challenging, as unwanted artifacts could lead to incorrect feature extraction. This justifies bandpass filtering and normalization application before feeding the signals into the model. As seen in Figure 1, the raw ECG signal contains baseline drift and high-frequency noise, which must be removed to ensure reliable classification. Figure 2 presents the same ECG signal after preprocessing. The bandpass filter removed baseline drift, and normalization ensured consistent amplitude distribution, improving signal quality for classification. By comparing Figure 1 and Figure 2, we observe that noise and baseline wander have been significantly reduced, making the signal cleaner and more suitable for deep-learning _Figure 1._ Raw ECG signals for a 10-second recording across three leads with wander baseline and noise.

The MUSIC and I-Care datasets were combined to leverage the strengths of both datasets. The MUSIC dataset provided an imbalanced representation of No-risk and At-risk patients, while the I-Care dataset enriched the At-risk class with additional samples. This integration was achieved by augmenting the MUSIC dataset with At-risk samples from I-Care. This ensured the model was exposed to various ECG patterns associated with cardiac arrest risk. One key challenge was the variation in lead configurations between the datasets. The MUSIC dataset contains three-lead ECG recordings, while the I-Care dataset comprises single-lead recordings. To integrate them, we duplicated the single I-Care lead across three channels, making it consistent with MUSIC’s structure. Since I-Care does not specify lead types, the final dataset was treated as a six-lead input, ensuring no loss of signal information. This approach allowed the datasets to be harmonized without assuming any correspondence between the leads, thereby addressing the variability in lead configurations across the datasets. 3.5.2. **Model Training and Fine-Tuning**

chunks.raw_text: The training pipeline was designed to fine-tune a pre-trained deep-learning model for predicting cardiac arrest using the combined MUSIC and I-Care datasets. The model utilized pre-trained weights from a 12-lead ECG classification model. To retain previously learned features while adapting to the new task, the first five layers were frozen, and the remaining layers were fine-tuned. The Adam optimizer, with a learning rate of 0.001 and a binary cross-entropy loss function, is used for training and was suitable for binary classification tasks. The training was performed for up to 100 epochs with a batch size of 32, using a custom data generator (ECGSequence) for efficient data loading and preprocessing. Callbacks such as ReduceLROnPlateau (reducing the learning rate when validation loss plateaued), EarlyStopping (halting training after 15 epochs without improvement), and ModelCheckpoint (saving the best model based on validation loss) were implemented to ensure robust training. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, and AUC metrics, providing a comprehensive assessment of its ability to distinguish between No-risk and At-risk samples. The training and validation metrics were logged and visualized to monitor convergence and detect potential overfitting. Several training strategies were explored: training from scratch, multi-task learning (MTL), and single-task learning (STL). The most effective approach was transfer learning with STL, demonstrating superior performance on the combined datasets.

chunks.raw_text: The transfer learning framework utilized a pre-trained ResNet-based model originally developed for 12-lead ECG classification. The model, trained on over 2.3 million ECG recordings from the Telehealth Network of Minas Gerais (TNMG) in Brazil, achieved F1 scores above 80% and specificity over 99%, surpassing cardiology residents’ performance in detecting a wide range of abnormalities, including atrial fibrillation (AF), bundle branch blocks, sinus bradycardia (SB), and sinus tachycardia (ST), as described by Ribeiro et al. (2020) [5]. The original ResNet architecture, designed for one-dimensional ECG signals, consists of 1D convolutional layers for time-series processing, residual units with skip connections to enhance gradient flow, batch normalization for stable training, and dropout layers to reduce overfitting. These components enable robust classification of 12-lead ECG data. Since our dataset consists of 6-lead ECG inputs, the pre-trained model must be modified to ensure compatibility. The first convolutional layer is adjusted to accept six input channels instead of 12, retaining only the relevant pre-trained weights while discarding the remaining ones. The first 5 layers are frozen to leverage existing knowledge, preserving general ECG waveform features. In contrast, the deeper layers are fine-tuned to specialize in the binary classification of cardiac arrest risk (At-risk vs. No-risk). This transfer learning strategy reduces the need for extensive retraining while effectively adapting the model to the new dataset. The adapted architecture maintains key structural components from the original model, ensuring flexibility for various ECG datasets and tasks. These modifications allow the model to retain valuable features learned from large-scale ECG datasets while adapting to reduced-lead inputs. Freezing the early layers preserved general waveform representations while fine-tuning deeper layers enabled cardiac arrest risk classification specialization. This efficient training strategy provides improved performance compared to training from scratch. As shown in Table 3, these modifications allow the model to retain valuable features learned from large-scale ECG datasets while adapting to reduced-lead inputs. Freezing the early layers preserved general representations of ECG waveforms while fine-tuning the deeper layers helped the model specialize in cardiac arrest risk classification. This strategy ensures efficient training and improved performance compared to training from scratch. **Step** **Modification** **Reason**

chunks.raw_text: _Figure 3._ Residual neural network architecture adapted for ECG classification. The architecture includes a Conv1D layer, BatchNorm, ReLU activation, residual units with skip connections, dropout, and a final dense layer with a binary classification function.

Figure 3 illustrates the adapted ResNet model for ECG classification. The input signal first passes through a Conv1D layer with 64 filters and a kernel size of 16, followed by Batch Normalization (BatchNorm) to stabilize training and a ReLU activation function to introduce non-linearity. Next, the model contains four Residual Units, each comprising Conv1D, BatchNorm, ReLU activation, and Dropout layers. After the residual units, the feature maps are passed through a flattened layer, followed by a fully connected Dense layer that refines learned representations. Finally, a sigmoid activation function generates the binary classification output (At-risk vs. No-risk).

chunks.raw_text: The model achieved strong performance on a combined MUSIC and I-Care ECG recordings dataset by adapting a pre-trained ResNet-based model initially developed for 12-lead ECG classification [5]. The final model attained an AUC of 0.8908, an accuracy of 87.90%, and a precision of 0.8727, showcasing its ability to generalize effectively to unseen data. These results highlight the efficacy of transfer learning in leveraging knowledge from largescale 12-lead ECG datasets to improve performance on reduced-lead configurations, increasing its applicability in real-world scenarios such as intensive care units and wearable devices. Integrating the complementary MUSIC and I-Care datasets allowed the study to address key challenges, including class imbalance, fragmented recordings, and varying sampling rates. The model could accurately distinguish between No-risk and At-risk patients through preprocessing and transfer learning, contributing to the growing field of AI-driven cardiovascular risk assessment. This work provides a practical solution for early cardiac arrest detection, potentially enhancing patient outcomes.

triples.o: combined MUSIC and I-Care ECG recordings dataset
ability to generalize effectively to unseen data
practical solution for early cardiac arrest detection

chunks.raw_text: While the results are promising, this study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. One major limitation is dataset constraints. The MUSIC dataset is relatively small and highly imbalanced, with significantly fewer At-risk samples compared to No-risk ones. Similarly, the I-Care dataset lacks explicit lead information, requiring assumptions during preprocessing. These limitations may reduce the model’s ability to generalize to other populations or clinical settings. Another concern is the reduced-lead configuration. Although the model was adapted for 6-lead ECG data, it was originally pre-trained on 12-lead inputs. While padding and transfer learning helped bridge this gap, the model’s true performance on native 6-lead recordings remains uncertain. This raises questions about its accuracy when applied to datasets with genuine 6-lead ECG data. Finally, the model has limited real-world validation. Its effectiveness has not yet been tested in clinical settings, which limits its practical applicability in real-world medical decision-making.

model's ability to generalize to clinical settings
model's accuracy on genuine 6-lead ECG data
practical applicability in real-world medical decision-making

chunks.raw_text: Several key directions are proposed to address the current study’s limitations and further advance AI-driven cardiac arrest prediction. First, future studies should incorporate larger and more diverse datasets, particularly native 6-lead ECG recordings, to improve generalizability and reduce potential biases arising from differences in patient populations and ECG acquisition protocols. Collaborations with clinical institutions will be essential for accessing high-quality, representative data. Second, the current assumption that duplicated single-lead data can substitute for multilead ECGs should be tested. Future studies will evaluate model performance across native 1-lead, 3-lead, and 6-lead ECG inputs to test the assumption that lead duplication preserves diagnostic value. This will help determine the role of lead-specific features in cardiac arrest risk prediction.

triples.o: duplicated single-lead data can substitute for multilead ECGs
model performance across native 1-lead, 3-lead, and 6-lead ECG inputs
role of lead-specific features in cardiac arrest risk prediction

chunks.raw_text: Third, alternative architectures such as EfficientNet and Transformer-based models will be explored to evaluate potential gains in performance and computational efficiency compared to ResNet. Additionally, model calibration will be evaluated using metrics such as Expected Calibration Error (ECE) to ensure that predicted risk probabilities are reliable for clinical decision-making. Finally, the feasibility of deploying the model on wearable devices will be investigated. As wearable ECG monitors become increasingly common, future research will assess model performance on reduced-lead ECG data collected in ambulatory settings and benchmark inference time, memory usage, and power consumption on embedded hardware. By addressing these areas, future work can build on the foundation established in this study. These advancements will improve model performance and clinical utility and pave the way for broader adoption of AI-driven solutions in cardiovascular risk assessment.
